title: The tyranny of authenticity
model: Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading Part 5 (extended text, multiple choice)
text:
Few injunctions are repeated as insistently in contemporary culture as the command to 'be yourself'. Advertisers urge us to express our true identity through the products we buy; self-help books promise to strip away the masks imposed by society and reveal the authentic person beneath; politicians are praised less for the coherence of their policies than for seeming 'real'. Authenticity has become, in the words of one critic, the closest thing our secular age has to a moral absolute. It is worth pausing to ask whether this ideal is quite as liberating as it appears.
The notion that each of us possesses an inner, essential self, waiting to be discovered and expressed, is of relatively recent vintage. For much of history, a person's identity was understood largely in terms of their roles and obligations: as a member of a family, a guild, a religious community or a social class. The question 'Who am I really?' would have struck many of our ancestors as faintly absurd. It was the Romantic movement of the late eighteenth century, with its veneration of individual feeling and its suspicion of convention, that elevated sincerity and self-expression into virtues of the first order.
The ideal has undoubtedly brought gains. It has encouraged people to resist conformity, to question inherited prejudices and to pursue lives that reflect their own convictions rather than the expectations of others. Movements for the rights of minorities have drawn much of their moral force from the claim that people should not be compelled to conceal who they are.
Yet the ideal also harbours paradoxes. If the self is something to be discovered, it is far from clear where one should look. Introspection is notoriously unreliable; psychological research has repeatedly shown that we are poor judges of our own motives and readily construct plausible stories after the fact. Moreover, the self that we 'find' turns out to be suspiciously similar to the selves on offer in the surrounding culture. The teenager who rebels against convention by adopting a particular style of dress is, more often than not, joining a different convention.
Social media have intensified these tensions. Platforms reward users for presenting a distinctive, consistent and appealing persona, while simultaneously penalising any hint of artifice. The result is a peculiar form of labour: the effortful performance of effortlessness. Influencers carefully stage 'unfiltered' moments; candid confessions are drafted and redrafted. Authenticity, once conceived as the opposite of performance, has become one of its most marketable genres.
Perhaps the deepest problem, however, is that the cult of authenticity can make change seem like betrayal. If I am obliged to be true to an essential self, then any attempt to become different, more patient, more generous, more disciplined, risks being dismissed as pretence. Aristotle, by contrast, held that we become virtuous by practising virtue, acting as a courageous person would until courage becomes second nature. On this view, character is not uncovered but cultivated, and there is nothing inauthentic about striving to be someone one is not yet.
None of this is to argue for a return to rigid social roles or to deny the value of sincerity. It is rather to suggest that the self may be better understood as a project than as a buried treasure. The question worth asking is perhaps not 'Who am I really?' but 'Who is it worth trying to become?'

title: The replication crisis
model: Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
In 2015, a consortium of some two hundred and seventy researchers published the results of an ambitious undertaking. They had attempted to repeat one hundred studies previously published in leading psychology journals, following the original methods as closely as possible. The outcome sent tremors through the discipline: fewer than forty per cent of the replications produced results consistent with the originals. Findings that had been cited in textbooks, discussed in popular books and used to inform public policy suddenly appeared to rest on remarkably shaky foundations.
The so-called replication crisis has since been shown to extend well beyond psychology, affecting fields as diverse as medicine, economics and cancer biology. Its causes are many, but few involve outright fraud. The more insidious problem lies in a set of practices that, until recently, were widely regarded as harmless or even routine.
Consider the incentives facing a typical researcher. Careers depend on publication, and journals have historically favoured studies reporting striking, statistically significant effects over those that find nothing. Faced with a disappointing result, a researcher might, quite innocently, try analysing the data in a slightly different way, exclude a few participants who seem to have misunderstood the instructions, or collect a little more data before checking again. Each decision may appear defensible in isolation. Cumulatively, however, they dramatically increase the probability of obtaining a 'significant' result by chance alone, a practice that has come to be known as 'p-hacking'. Meanwhile, studies that fail to find an effect are quietly filed away and never published, so that the scientific literature presents a systematically distorted picture of reality.
Small sample sizes have compounded the problem. A study involving thirty undergraduates may detect an effect that is, in truth, a statistical fluke, and because such studies are cheap and quick, they can proliferate. Some of the most celebrated findings in social psychology, from the notion that briefly adopting a 'power pose' boosts confidence to the claim that willpower is a finite resource that can be depleted, have struggled to survive larger and more rigorous attempts at replication.
It would be a mistake, though, to conclude that science is fundamentally broken. On the contrary, the crisis is itself a product of science's capacity for self-correction: it was scientists, after all, who designed the replication projects and publicised their sobering results. The response has been considerable. Many journals now encourage or require 'pre-registration', in which researchers publicly specify their hypotheses and methods before collecting data, making it far harder to adjust the analysis after the fact. Some journals have adopted 'registered reports', agreeing to publish a study on the basis of its design, regardless of what it eventually finds. Data-sharing has become increasingly common, and large collaborative projects pooling participants from dozens of laboratories have begun to replace small, isolated studies.
The episode nonetheless carries lessons for the wider public. A single study, however intriguing, rarely settles a question, and the more surprising a finding is, the more scepticism it warrants until it has been independently confirmed. Journalists, policymakers and readers alike would do well to treat headlines announcing that 'scientists have discovered' something with a measure of patience. Science advances not through isolated revelations but through the slow, often unglamorous accumulation of evidence, and through a willingness to discard ideas, however appealing, that fail to withstand scrutiny.

title: On translation
model: Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
There is an Italian saying, traduttore, traditore, 'translator, traitor', that neatly encapsulates the suspicion with which translation has long been regarded. The phrase itself illustrates the problem: its pleasing echo, the near-identity of the two words, evaporates the moment it is rendered into English. Something is inevitably lost. And yet, without translation, most readers would never encounter Homer, Tolstoy or García Márquez, and our sense of what literature can be would be immeasurably poorer. The question is not whether translation betrays its original, for in some sense it always does, but what kind of betrayal is worth committing.
Translators have traditionally been caught between two loyalties. On the one hand lies fidelity to the source: to its precise meanings, its structure, its strangeness. On the other lies fidelity to the reader, who must be offered a text that reads naturally in their own language. The German theologian Friedrich Schleiermacher framed the dilemma memorably in 1813: the translator, he argued, can either leave the writer in peace and move the reader towards him, or leave the reader in peace and move the writer towards the reader. Schleiermacher himself favoured the former, believing that a translation should retain a trace of the foreign, reminding readers that they are encountering another culture rather than a disguised version of their own.
In practice, most translators navigate between these poles from sentence to sentence. Puns, idioms and cultural references pose particular difficulties. Should a joke that depends on a play on words be translated literally, and thus lose its humour, or replaced by a different joke that works in the target language, and thus lose its connection to the original? Should a reference to a local dish or festival be explained, adapted or left unexplained, trusting the reader to infer its significance? Poetry, in which sound, rhythm and meaning are inseparable, represents the extreme case; Robert Frost reputedly defined poetry as 'what gets lost in translation'.
The historical record offers striking examples of translations that took enormous liberties. Edward FitzGerald's nineteenth-century version of the Rubáiyát of Omar Khayyám rearranged, combined and freely reinvented the Persian quatrains on which it was based, yet it became one of the best-loved poems in the English language. Some scholars regard it as a travesty; others consider it a masterpiece in its own right. Its success raises the uncomfortable possibility that a 'faithful' translation and a great one are not necessarily the same thing.
In recent years, the status of translators has begun to change. Once largely invisible, their names relegated to the small print, they increasingly appear on book covers, and prizes now reward translator and author jointly. This recognition reflects a growing awareness that translation is not a mechanical transfer of meaning from one code to another but a creative act requiring judgement, sensitivity and considerable literary skill.
The advent of machine translation has, paradoxically, reinforced this point. Automated systems have become remarkably proficient at conveying the gist of everyday texts. Yet literary translators argue that their work lies precisely in those areas where machines struggle: in tone, irony, ambiguity and the countless small decisions through which a voice is recreated in another language. If translation is a form of betrayal, it is one that demands a deep and paradoxical loyalty.

title: Growth and its discontents
model: Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
For more than seventy years, the health of national economies has been judged primarily by a single figure: gross domestic product, the total value of goods and services produced within a country. Governments rise and fall on the strength of its fluctuations; news bulletins report quarterly growth rates with the solemnity once reserved for military communiqués. Yet the very economist who helped develop the measure, Simon Kuznets, warned the United States Congress in 1934 that 'the welfare of a nation can scarcely be inferred from a measurement of national income'. His caution has been largely ignored.
The limitations of GDP are well known. It counts activity, not wellbeing. A car accident, which generates spending on repairs, medical treatment and legal fees, adds to GDP; so does the clean-up after an oil spill. Conversely, a great deal of what makes life worthwhile is invisible to it. The unpaid work of caring for children and elderly relatives, overwhelmingly performed by women, does not register at all. Nor does leisure, so that a society which chose to work fewer hours and enjoy more free time would appear, by this measure, to be getting poorer. GDP also says nothing about how income is distributed: an economy can grow briskly while the majority of its citizens see their living standards stagnate.
The most consequential blind spot, however, concerns the natural world. GDP treats the depletion of forests, fisheries and fossil fuels as income rather than as the running down of capital, much as if a household were to count the sale of its furniture as salary. As the ecological costs of growth have become harder to ignore, a lively debate has emerged about whether continued expansion of economic output is compatible with the limits of the planet.
One camp, advocating 'green growth', argues that technological innovation can 'decouple' prosperity from environmental damage. They point to countries that have managed to reduce carbon emissions while their economies continued to expand, largely by switching from coal to renewable energy. A more radical camp, associated with the idea of 'degrowth', contends that such decoupling has been neither fast enough nor broad enough to avert ecological breakdown, and that wealthy nations must deliberately scale back material consumption, redirecting their efforts towards wellbeing, equality and public services rather than ever-greater output.
Critics of degrowth counter that it is politically unrealistic and potentially cruel, given that growth has lifted hundreds of millions of people out of extreme poverty and that recessions, which are in effect episodes of unplanned degrowth, are invariably accompanied by unemployment and hardship. Proponents reply that they are not advocating recession but a planned transition, and that their proposals apply chiefly to rich countries, whose consumption far exceeds what is needed for a good life.
Between these positions, a broader consensus has emerged that GDP alone is an inadequate compass. New Zealand has introduced a 'wellbeing budget' that evaluates policies according to their effects on health, the environment and social cohesion, while several countries now publish dashboards of indicators alongside traditional economic statistics. Whether such initiatives will genuinely alter priorities, or merely decorate them, remains to be seen. What is clear is that the question of what an economy is for, long treated as settled, has been reopened.

title: The uses of nostalgia
model: Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
In 1688, a Swiss medical student named Johannes Hofer coined a new term to describe a condition he had observed among soldiers serving far from home. Combining the Greek words for 'return home' and 'pain', he called it nostalgia, and he regarded it as a potentially fatal disease. Its symptoms reportedly included melancholy, loss of appetite, fever and an obsessive preoccupation with thoughts of one's native land. For the next two centuries, physicians proposed a bewildering array of remedies, from leeches and opium to a trip to the Swiss Alps. Some military commanders went further, threatening soldiers who displayed symptoms with severe punishment.
Over time, the meaning of the word shifted. Nostalgia ceased to be a medical diagnosis and came to denote a wistful longing not for a place but for a time: the lost world of one's childhood, or a vanished era one may never have experienced at all. For much of the twentieth century it retained negative connotations, viewed by psychologists as a form of escapism or even a symptom of depression.
Research over the past two decades has painted a strikingly different picture. Studies led by the psychologist Constantine Sedikides and his colleagues suggest that nostalgia, far from being debilitating, typically serves valuable psychological functions. When people are invited to recall nostalgic memories, they tend to report higher self-esteem, a stronger sense of social connection and a greater feeling that their lives are meaningful. Nostalgic memories usually centre on significant events shared with loved ones, and although they are tinged with sadness at the passing of time, the predominant emotion is positive. Intriguingly, people appear to turn to nostalgia more frequently when they feel lonely, anxious or uncertain, suggesting that it may act as a kind of emotional resource, drawn upon in difficult moments to restore a sense of continuity.
Yet nostalgia also has a more problematic side, particularly when it moves from the personal to the collective. Political movements of many persuasions have exploited a yearning for an idealised past, promising to restore a former greatness that was, in reality, considerably more complicated than the slogans suggest. Such appeals tend to edit out the inconvenient: the poverty, disease and exclusion that marked the 'good old days' for large sections of the population. The historian Svetlana Boym drew a useful distinction between what she called 'restorative' nostalgia, which seeks to rebuild the lost home and treats the past as a truth to be defended, and 'reflective' nostalgia, which dwells on longing itself, aware of the ambiguities of memory and the impossibility of return.
The commercial world, too, has discovered nostalgia's power. Film studios revive franchises from decades ago; brands reissue products in their original packaging; music from the past is endlessly repackaged. Critics worry that a culture saturated with recycled memories may find it harder to imagine genuinely new futures.
The paradox of nostalgia, then, is that the same emotion which can console an individual and strengthen bonds between people can, on a larger scale, distort our understanding of history. Perhaps the lesson is not to resist nostalgia, which seems to be an enduring part of human experience, but to cultivate the reflective variety: to cherish the past without mistaking it for a place to which we might return.

title: The attention economy
model: Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
In 1971, the economist and psychologist Herbert Simon made an observation that now seems prophetic. 'A wealth of information', he wrote, 'creates a poverty of attention.' Half a century later, his insight has become the organising principle of some of the most profitable companies in history. The services they provide, from search engines to social networks and video platforms, are offered free of charge. Their revenue derives instead from advertising, and advertising depends on one scarce commodity: the time and focus of users. We are not, as the oft-repeated phrase has it, the customers of these companies; we are the product being sold.
This business model creates powerful incentives to maximise 'engagement', the amount of time people spend on a platform and the frequency with which they return. To achieve it, designers have drawn extensively on behavioural psychology. Infinite scrolling removes natural stopping points; autoplay ensures that one video seamlessly follows another; notifications arrive at unpredictable intervals, exploiting the same principle of variable reward that makes slot machines so compelling. Several former employees of large technology firms have spoken publicly of their unease at having helped to build products deliberately engineered to be difficult to put down.
The algorithms that determine what users see are optimised for engagement rather than for accuracy, balance or wellbeing. Since content that provokes strong emotions, particularly outrage, tends to be shared more widely, critics argue that these systems inadvertently reward polarisation and sensationalism. The individual user experiences this as a personalised stream of irresistible material; the cumulative effect, some contend, is a public sphere fragmented into mutually incomprehensible camps.
The evidence on harms is, however, more contested than popular accounts sometimes suggest. Studies of the relationship between social media use and adolescent mental health, for instance, have produced conflicting results, with some finding substantial associations and others only modest ones. Disentangling cause from correlation is notoriously difficult: anxious teenagers may turn to their phones, rather than phones making teenagers anxious. Similarly, research on 'filter bubbles' suggests that many users are in fact exposed to a wider range of views online than offline. Responsible critics acknowledge these complexities, even as they argue that the burden of proof should rest with the companies rather than the public.
Responses have taken several forms. Some governments have introduced regulations requiring greater transparency about how algorithms work, restricting data collection, or imposing special protections for children. A growing 'humane technology' movement urges designers to build products that respect users' time and intentions, for example by making it easy to turn off recommendations or by displaying reminders when someone has been scrolling for a long period. At the individual level, many people have adopted strategies ranging from deleting applications to setting their phones to greyscale, which reportedly makes them markedly less appealing.
Ultimately, the debate turns on a question that extends beyond technology: who should control the direction of our attention? Attention, as the philosopher Simone Weil observed, is the rarest and purest form of generosity. It shapes what we notice, what we care about and, in the end, who we become. Whether we allow it to be harvested as raw material for advertising, or insist on reclaiming it, may prove one of the defining choices of our era.

title: The placebo puzzle
model: Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
During the Second World War, as supplies of morphine ran out in a field hospital in Italy, an American anaesthetist named Henry Beecher reportedly witnessed something that would shape his career. A nurse, lacking the real drug, injected a wounded soldier with a simple salt solution while assuring him that it was a powerful painkiller. To Beecher's astonishment, the soldier's agony subsided. After the war, Beecher went on to publish an influential paper arguing that a substantial proportion of patients improve after receiving treatments that contain no active ingredient whatsoever. The 'placebo effect' had entered mainstream medicine.
Today, the placebo occupies a curious position. On the one hand, it is regarded as a nuisance: the background noise that clinical trials must eliminate in order to establish whether a new drug genuinely works. On the other, it has become an object of fascination in its own right, offering a window into the intricate relationship between mind and body.
Research over recent decades has demonstrated that placebo responses are far from imaginary. Brain imaging studies have shown that, in some patients, placebo painkillers trigger the release of the body's own pain-relieving chemicals, endorphins, and that this effect can be blocked by drugs that counteract opiates. In patients with Parkinson's disease, placebos have been found to stimulate the release of dopamine. The context of treatment matters enormously. Two placebo pills tend to work better than one; injections often outperform pills; expensive placebos appear more effective than cheap ones; and the warmth and confidence of a doctor can significantly amplify the response.
The effect also has a sinister twin: the 'nocebo'. Patients who are warned about possible side effects of a medication frequently report experiencing them, even when they are in fact receiving an inert substance. In some trials, significant numbers of participants in the placebo group have withdrawn because of side effects they attributed to the treatment. This poses a genuine dilemma for doctors, who are ethically obliged to inform patients of risks, yet may inadvertently induce symptoms by doing so.
Perhaps the most surprising recent finding concerns so-called 'open-label' placebos. In several studies, patients with conditions such as irritable bowel syndrome and chronic back pain were given pills explicitly described as containing no medication, along with an explanation of how placebos can work. Many nevertheless reported meaningful improvements. If confirmed, such results would challenge the long-standing assumption that deception is essential to the placebo effect, and might open the way to its ethical use in clinical practice.
It is important not to overstate what placebos can achieve. They can influence symptoms such as pain, nausea and fatigue, which are shaped by the brain's interpretation of bodily signals, but there is no reliable evidence that they shrink tumours or cure infections. Promoters of dubious therapies sometimes invoke the placebo effect to justify treatments that lack any specific benefit, a move that risks diverting patients from effective care.
The enduring lesson of Beecher's observation is perhaps not that belief can cure disease, but that healing is never a purely mechanical process. The meaning a patient attaches to treatment, the trust they place in their carers and the expectations they bring are themselves part of the medicine.

title: Museums and the question of return
model: Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
In the galleries of the great museums of Europe and North America, visitors can admire treasures gathered from every corner of the globe: Egyptian mummies, Greek sculptures, bronze plaques from the kingdom of Benin, ceremonial objects from the Pacific. For much of the past two centuries, these institutions have presented themselves as guardians of a shared human heritage, preserving fragile artefacts and making them accessible to millions. In recent years, however, that self-image has come under sustained challenge, as countries and communities from which many objects were taken have demanded their return.
The circumstances under which artefacts entered museum collections vary enormously. Some were purchased legitimately, excavated with permission or given as gifts. Others, however, were acquired through conquest, coercion or outright plunder. The most frequently cited example is the Benin Bronzes, thousands of sculptures and plaques seized by British forces during a punitive military expedition in 1897, which destroyed much of Benin City in what is now Nigeria. The objects were subsequently sold to cover the costs of the expedition and dispersed among museums and private collections around the world.
Those who resist calls for restitution have advanced several arguments. They contend that objects acquired in accordance with the laws and norms of their time should not be judged by contemporary standards, and that 'universal museums', which display the achievements of many civilisations side by side, foster understanding between cultures. Concerns have also been raised about whether some recipient countries possess the facilities to conserve delicate items, and about the precedent that large-scale returns might set: if one object is returned, it is asked, where would the process end? In some countries, laws explicitly prohibit national museums from permanently removing items from their collections.
Advocates of return find many of these arguments unconvincing. The appeal to the norms of the time, they point out, ignores the fact that the people from whom objects were taken never accepted those norms. The claim that artefacts are safer in Western museums is undermined by the construction of modern museums in many of the countries concerned, and by occasional incidents of theft and damage in European institutions themselves. Above all, they argue, the issue is not merely one of ownership but of dignity: the ability of communities to tell their own histories through objects that were integral to their religious, political and artistic life.
The tide appears to be turning. Following a report commissioned by the French president in 2018, France returned a number of objects to Benin and Senegal. Germany has agreed to transfer ownership of hundreds of Benin Bronzes to Nigeria, and several universities and museums have voluntarily returned items. Arrangements vary: some objects have been returned outright, while others remain on display abroad under long-term loans negotiated with their countries of origin.
Whatever the outcome of individual disputes, the debate has prompted a broader reflection on the role of museums. Many have begun to research the provenance of their collections more rigorously, to acknowledge the violence that sometimes lay behind them, and to collaborate with source communities on how objects are interpreted. The museum of the future may be less a treasure house than a meeting place, one in which the question of whose story is being told is never far from view.

title: The wisdom and folly of crowds
model: Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
In 1906, the scientist Francis Galton attended a livestock fair in the west of England, where visitors were invited to guess the weight of an ox once it had been slaughtered and dressed. Galton, who held a notoriously low opinion of the intelligence of ordinary people, collected the eight hundred or so entries expecting to demonstrate the folly of the crowd. Instead, he found that the median estimate was within one per cent of the true weight, closer than the guesses of most individual experts. The episode has since become the founding parable of what the journalist James Surowiecki termed 'the wisdom of crowds'.
The principle behind it is statistical rather than mystical. When many people make independent estimates, their individual errors, some too high and some too low, tend to cancel each other out, leaving an average that converges on the truth. This logic underpins a range of modern practices, from prediction markets, in which participants bet on the outcome of elections or economic events, to the aggregation of user reviews and the design of certain forecasting tournaments.
Crucially, however, the effect depends on several conditions, and when these are absent, the crowd can be spectacularly wrong. The first is diversity: participants must bring different information and perspectives to the problem. The second, and perhaps most important, is independence. If people are influenced by one another's opinions, their errors cease to be random and begin to align. A famous series of experiments in the 1950s by the psychologist Solomon Asch showed that individuals would frequently deny the evidence of their own eyes, agreeing that obviously unequal lines were the same length, simply because everyone else in the room had said so. More recent research has demonstrated that when participants in estimation tasks are shown the guesses of others, the diversity of their answers shrinks dramatically, while their confidence increases, and their collective accuracy frequently deteriorates.
The consequences extend well beyond the laboratory. Financial bubbles, from seventeenth-century tulip mania to the dot-com boom, can be understood as failures of independence, in which investors bought assets not because of their underlying value but because others were buying them. Within organisations, the phenomenon of 'groupthink', a term coined by the psychologist Irving Janis, describes how cohesive teams can suppress dissent and converge on disastrous decisions, as in a number of notorious foreign policy fiascos. Online, the visible accumulation of likes and shares can create cascades in which early popularity, rather than quality, determines which ideas spread.
How, then, can groups harness collective intelligence while avoiding its pitfalls? Researchers suggest a number of practical measures. Asking individuals to record their judgements privately before any discussion helps to preserve independence. Appointing someone to argue deliberately against the prevailing view can surface overlooked objections. Leaders who announce their own opinion at the outset of a meeting, by contrast, risk anchoring everyone else's.
The lesson of Galton's ox, then, is more subtle than it first appears. Crowds are neither inherently wise nor inherently foolish. Their judgement depends less on the intelligence of their members than on the structure of their interactions, and that is something which can be deliberately designed.

title: The ethics of geoengineering
model: Cambridge C2 Proficiency – Reading Part 5 (extended text)
text:
In June 1991, Mount Pinatubo in the Philippines erupted with colossal force, ejecting some fifteen million tonnes of sulphur dioxide into the stratosphere. Over the following months, the resulting haze of tiny particles spread around the planet, reflecting a small fraction of incoming sunlight back into space. Global average temperatures fell by roughly half a degree Celsius, an effect that lasted for more than a year. For a growing number of scientists, the eruption offered a tantalising, and deeply unsettling, demonstration: humanity might, in principle, be able to cool the planet deliberately.
The idea, known as solar geoengineering, involves releasing reflective particles into the upper atmosphere, perhaps using specially designed high-altitude aircraft. Its advocates stress that it would not be a substitute for reducing greenhouse gas emissions but, at most, a temporary measure to limit the worst effects of warming while emissions are brought down. Preliminary estimates suggest that it could be remarkably cheap, costing a small fraction of what a rapid transition away from fossil fuels will require. That very cheapness, however, is one of the reasons it alarms its critics.
The objections are formidable. The first is scientific uncertainty. Climate is a staggeringly complex system, and models suggest that reducing sunlight would not simply reverse the effects of carbon dioxide. Rainfall patterns could be disrupted, with potentially devastating consequences for regions dependent on monsoons. Since geoengineering would not remove carbon from the atmosphere, it would do nothing to address ocean acidification, which threatens coral reefs and marine ecosystems.
A second objection concerns what has been called 'termination shock'. If an injection programme were sustained for decades while greenhouse gases continued to accumulate, and then abruptly halted, perhaps because of war, economic collapse or political disagreement, the masked warming would reassert itself within a few years, far too rapidly for ecosystems or societies to adapt.
Perhaps the most intractable problems, though, are political. Who would decide the global temperature? A measure that benefits one region might harm another, and there is no international institution with the authority to make such decisions, or to compensate those who might suffer. Because the technology could in principle be deployed by a single country, or even a wealthy individual, some fear it could become a source of conflict. Others worry about 'moral hazard': the mere prospect of a technological fix might weaken the political will to pursue the difficult and costly task of cutting emissions.
Supporters of research reply that these risks must be weighed against those of unmitigated climate change, which are themselves severe and increasingly certain. If the world fails to reduce emissions quickly enough, they argue, future governments facing catastrophic heatwaves may be tempted to resort to geoengineering in desperation. It would be far better for such decisions to be informed by careful research, conducted openly and under international oversight, than made in ignorance. Opponents counter that research itself creates momentum, normalising an intervention that should remain unthinkable, and several hundred academics have called for an international agreement not to use the technology.
The debate thus confronts humanity with an uncomfortable question. Having altered the climate inadvertently, should we contemplate altering it deliberately? There is no answer that is free of risk; the choice may lie only between different kinds of danger.
